statement: When a positive integer $n$ is divided by $3$, the whole-number quotient (ignoring any remainder) is the same as the whole-number quotient when $n$ is divided by $4$. For example, $n = 5$ works, because $5 \div 3$ and $5 \div 4$ both have quotient $1$. How many positive integers $n$ have this property?

hints: Try the first dozen values of $n$ and write down both quotients.
If the common quotient is $q$, then $n$ is at least $4q$ (to reach quotient $q$ when dividing by $4$) and at most $3q + 2$ (to stay below $q + 1$ when dividing by $3$).
So $4q \le n \le 3q + 2$, which is only possible when $q \le 2$. Check $q = 0, 1, 2$ one at a time.

solutions.reliable: Let the common quotient be $q$. Dividing by $4$ gives quotient $q$ exactly when $4q \le n \le 4q + 3$, and dividing by $3$ gives quotient $q$ exactly when $3q \le n \le 3q + 2$. Both hold when $4q \le n \le 3q + 2$, which needs $q \le 2$. For $q = 0$: $n = 1, 2$ (positive only). For $q = 1$: $4 \le n \le 5$. For $q = 2$: $8 \le n \le 8$. That is $n = 1, 2, 4, 5, 8$, so $5$ integers.
solutions.elegant: Dividing by $3$ throws away a remainder of at most $2$, so the quotient by $3$ is at least $\frac{n - 2}{3}$, while the quotient by $4$ is at most $\frac{n}{4}$. When $n > 8$ we have $4(n - 2) > 3n$, so $\frac{n - 2}{3} > \frac{n}{4}$ and the quotient by $3$ is strictly bigger. So only $n \le 8$ can work, and checking $1$ to $8$ finds $1, 2, 4, 5, 8$.
